data.BodyText:
David Shadle builds the systems that turn strategy into working software. Most advisors stop at the recommendation. He keeps going, through the model, the interface, and the handoff.

He is Technical Advisor, Product Strategy and UX at Banyan Software, working across a portfolio of more than 100 B2B SaaS operating companies. There he designed and built the product management platform the program runs on, and advised on and implemented the experience layer across three executive reporting products covering workshop performance, portfolio operations, and technology due diligence.

He works from a rulebook. The rules of a domain get written down once, in plain language, and the technical pieces are derived from that rather than maintained by hand. It is a working discipline, not a product, and it is what lets him carry a project through delivery rather than stopping at design.

Twenty five years in product strategy and design precede this, including principal roles at Microsoft and Oracle.

data.Label: Three hundred words

data.BodyText:
David Shadle builds the systems that turn strategy into working software. Most advisors stop at the recommendation. He keeps going, through the model, the interface, and the handoff, so the thing that gets agreed on is the thing that gets shipped.

He is Technical Advisor, Product Strategy and UX at Banyan Software, working across a portfolio of more than 100 B2B SaaS operating companies, supporting operating company teams, product management, and technology due diligence.

He designed and built the product management platform the program runs on, from concept through production. He advised on and implemented the experience layer across three executive reporting products: workshop maturity and performance, portfolio operations including cloud spend and compliance, and technology due diligence covering deal management and assignment. He rebuilt the Portfolio Operations dashboard onto a database backed foundation, replacing generated exports with live data. With his program team he co-led the redesign of the AI PM Workshop from a training curriculum into an execution engagement, where companies finish with a CEO signed strategy, a prioritized roadmap, and a ledger tracing decisions back to evidence.

His approach starts with the problem. Every engagement begins with a brief that proposes no solution, reviewed by the people who live with the problem, because alignment on the problem is what makes scoping and specification worth doing. From there he works from a rulebook: the rules of a domain written down once in plain language, with the technical pieces derived from that rather than maintained by hand. It is what lets him deliver complete projects rather than stopping at design and project management.

He uses agents as a tool inside the strategy work. Given the context of a specific problem, an agent can research, pressure test a position, and assemble the evidence a decision needs, which surfaces opportunities earlier and builds alignment before execution begins. On a recent engagement with an FDA cleared medical technology company focused on breast cancer prevention, an agent he built acted as domain expert across pilot program design, distribution opportunity, and insurance carrier risk.

Twenty five years in product strategy and design precede this, including principal roles at Microsoft and Oracle. Full stack product practitioner. Not just capable of wearing several hats at once, but confident delivering the outcome in each.

data.Heading: The problem comes first, and it gets its own document
data.BodyText:
Designing against a problem nobody agreed on is the most expensive mistake available. It is also the easiest one to make, because solutions are more interesting to discuss than problems.

So every engagement starts with a brief that contains no screens, no architecture, and no charts. Only the problem, who has it, what it costs, and how we would know it was solved. It gets reviewed by the people who live with the problem before anything else begins.

Doing this properly means real analysis, and the analysis tends to turn things up. On one engagement it surfaced that staging and production were serving two different dashboards. That was a byproduct, not the goal. The goal was an executive team aligned on the problem, which is what makes the scoping and the specification that follow worth doing.
data.ShortBodyText: Every engagement starts with a brief containing no screens, no architecture, and no charts. Designing against a problem nobody agreed on is the most expensive mistake available.

data.Heading: The model gets written down once
data.BodyText:
Most drift starts small. A chart computes its own version of a metric. The documentation describes last quarter's schema. Two teams use the same word for different things. Nobody decides to let a system fall out of sync. It happens between decisions.

So I work from a rulebook. The rules of a domain get written down once, in plain language the person who owns the business meaning can read, and the technical pieces are derived from that rather than maintained by hand. Consistency comes from derivation rather than discipline.

What matters here is not the method but what it changed. My responsibility used to end at design and project management, with development handed to someone else. Working this way, I can carry a project from concept through delivery.
data.ShortBodyText: I work from a rulebook. The rules of a domain get written down in plain language, and the technical pieces are derived from that rather than maintained by hand. Consistency comes from derivation rather than discipline. It is what lets me carry a project through delivery rather than stopping at design.

data.Heading: The interface performs no business calculation
data.BodyText:
Every number on screen traces back to a declared field. A chart that computes its own version of a metric is a defect, not a shortcut.

This sounds like an engineering rule. It is really a trust rule. The moment two surfaces can disagree about the same number, every surface becomes a thing to verify rather than a thing to use.
data.ShortBodyText: Every number traces back to a declared field. A chart that computes its own version of a metric is a defect.

data.Heading: It is faster to argue with a wrong sketch than a blank page
data.BodyText:
I build working prototypes early, with real structure and real copy, specifically so people can tell me what is wrong. A prototype is an alignment device, not a deliverable. It exists to be knocked down.

Open questions belong in the room, visible, not resolved quietly and presented as settled. If a review tells me the problem statement was materially wrong, that is the process working, not failing.
data.ShortBodyText: It is faster to argue with a wrong sketch than a blank page, so I build early and put open questions in the room rather than resolving them quietly.

data.Heading: The stages are named, and each one is done when its artifact exists
data.BodyText:
A stage is complete when its artifact exists and its exit criteria are met. Not when the conversation feels finished.

1. Problem brief. The problem, agreed, with no solution in it.
2. Experience design. What it feels like to use, before what it costs to build.
3. Rulebook. The domain written down once, confirmed by the person who owns the meaning.
4. Scope and specification. Every component tied back to something named in the rulebook.
5. Build. Derived where it can be, written where it cannot.
6. Validate and hand off. Tested against the rulebook, handed to a team that owns it.

Not every engagement runs all six. Every engagement runs them in this order.

data.Heading: I own the decisions. The team owns the work.
data.BodyText:
I work between executives, operating partners, and delivery teams, and I take ownership of the calls I make. If I set a direction and it turns out to be wrong, that is mine to say and mine to help fix. Putting open questions in the room is not hedging. It is how you get to a decision you can stand behind.

Handing the work back is not stepping away from it. The measure of whether the work was any good is whether it still runs after I am gone. So it gets written in language the people who own it can read, and what gets handed over is whatever that team needs to carry it forward. That is a judgment call each time, not a package.
data.ShortBodyText: I stand behind the calls I make, and if one is wrong that is mine to say and mine to help fix. Handing the work back is not stepping away. The measure of whether it was any good is whether it still runs after I am gone.

data.Heading: Where AI fits
data.BodyText:
I use agents as a tool inside the strategy work, not as an end in themselves.

Given the context of a specific engagement, an agent can do real research, pressure test a position, and assemble the evidence a decision actually needs. That gets me to the problem faster. It surfaces opportunities I would not have found working alone. And it puts something concrete in front of stakeholders early enough to build alignment on the strategy before execution starts, which is when alignment is cheap.

They also changed how I think, which matters more. An agent does exactly what you specify, so vague thinking shows up immediately in the output. You learn to state the job, what a good result looks like, and what the rules are, before anything runs. I do that at the start of strategy work now, long before there is anything to build.
data.ShortBodyText: Given the context of an engagement, an agent can research, pressure test a position, and assemble evidence. That gets me to the problem faster and builds alignment before execution starts, when alignment is cheap.

data.Title: The rulebook approach (the through line)
data.ProblemText: Most drift starts small. A chart computes its own version of a metric. The documentation describes last quarter's schema. Two teams use the same word for different things. Nobody decides to let a system fall out of sync, it happens between decisions.
data.ActionText: Works from a rulebook. The rules of a domain get written down once, in plain language the person who owns the business meaning can read, and the technical pieces are derived from that rather than maintained by hand.
data.OutcomeText: It made him materially more productive. Previously the responsibility ended at design and project management, with development handed to someone else. Working this way, a project can be carried from concept through delivery by one person. That is the claim. Not that the method is novel.
data.AttributionNote: His working method, not his invention. Described, never sold.
data.RegisterNote: Describe, do not sell. Two or three sentences max, never a section. Never name transpilers, toolchains, or vendors. Safe line, use sparingly and never more than once per document: 'Consistency comes from derivation rather than discipline.'

data.Title: Product management platform, concept through production
data.ProblemText: A program serving more than 100 operating companies had no home. Content, coaching, assessment, and deliverables were scattered.
data.ActionText: Designed and built the platform end to end: personas and access model, corporate SSO, frontend, API, PostgreSQL, content and artifact layer, and containerized infrastructure with automated deployment. Content and navigation are data rather than code, so the product and its specification cannot drift apart.
data.OutcomeText: Live in production, serving PMs, operating partners, delivery coordinators, and program leads.
data.AttributionNote: Sole responsibility, concept through production. Language to use: 'Designed and built end to end.'
data.RegisterNote: The single strongest artifact in the record. Sole responsibility, concept to production.

data.Title: Training curriculum rebuilt as an execution engagement
data.ProblemText: Inherited a module based program. Companies completed a course and went back to work unchanged.
data.ActionText: Co-led the redesign with the program team: replaced the module sequence with a concept library surfaced at the point of need, removed hard gates in favor of facilitator judgment, capped CEO time at three to four hours.
data.OutcomeText: Companies now finish with four artifacts they own, including a CEO signed strategy, a prioritized and capacity validated roadmap, a customer facing roadmap, and a ledger tracing every decision back to evidence.
data.AttributionNote: Co-led with the program team. Language to use: 'Co-led the redesign.'
data.RegisterNote: Line worth keeping: 'You don't take the program and then go build your roadmap. You build your roadmap in the program.'

data.Title: Experience layer across three executive reporting products
data.ProblemText: Three audiences needed three different questions answered from the same portfolio: workshop maturity, participation and performance; portfolio operations covering cloud spend, escrow and compliance; and technology due diligence covering deal management, time tracking and assignment. Portfolio Operations was also fed by generated exports, so the numbers described a moment already past.
data.ActionText: Advised on and implemented the experience layer across all three, including interaction design, information architecture, and how the underlying data comes together. Rebuilt the Portfolio Operations dashboard onto a database backed foundation, replacing generated exports with live data and improving performance.
data.OutcomeText: Three products, each built for its own audience and its own question, with Portfolio Operations now reporting current state rather than the last export.
data.AttributionNote: Precisely: 'Advised on and implemented the experience layer.' Not owned. Did not own the estate, the data platform, or the engineering. The Portfolio Operations rebuild onto live data is his outright. Do not say 'five reporting surfaces' - there are three products.
data.RegisterNote: The three products: PM Workshop (operating partners, program leads, participants), Portfolio Operations (finance and executive), Technical Due Diligence (corporate development and diligence teams).

data.Title: A project brief that aligned executives and surfaced a process breakdown
data.ProblemText: The diligence reporting product needed rebuilding, and there was no agreed statement of what was actually wrong with it or what the rebuild was for.
data.ActionText: Wrote a project brief for executive review. It identified the opportunities, named the current gaps, and stated the problem without proposing a solution. Alignment on the brief is what leads to scoping, and scoping leads to a spec for execution.
data.OutcomeText: An executive team aligned on the problem before anyone designed against it. The analysis behind the brief also surfaced a non-trivial breakdown in process: staging and production were serving two different dashboards.
data.RegisterNote: The staging/production finding was a byproduct of doing the analysis properly, not a detective story. Overselling it turns a sound process into a boast. The value is the sequence: brief, alignment, scope, spec, execution.

data.Title: AI agents that scale one expert across a portfolio
data.ProblemText: Expert product coaching cannot sit inside a hundred companies at once. An AI coach can, but only if it teaches the same program the rest of the engagement runs on.
data.ActionText: Advisory. Defined how the AI coach had to align to the program, what it was accountable for teaching, and how it fits the participant's path through the portal. Set the boundary between what the coach handles and what the platform handles.
data.OutcomeText: An on demand coach that reinforces the program instead of competing with it, reached through the portal at the point in the journey where the participant needs it.
data.AttributionNote: Advisory only. The coach, skills toolkit, and maturity model were built by others. Contribution is program alignment and integration design. Must not imply authorship of the agents themselves.
data.RegisterNote: Demonstrates knowing what an AI product is accountable for, and where it stops. That judgment is the scarce part.

data.Title: Agents used to sharpen strategy before execution
data.ProblemText: Strategy work is limited by how much context one person can absorb and how much evidence they can assemble before a decision has to be made, which usually produces a position argued from partial information or alignment attempted after execution has already started.
data.ActionText: Uses agents as a tool inside the engagement to research the context, pressure test a position, and assemble evidence, so problems and opportunities are identified accurately and alignment is built before execution starts. Worked example: for an FDA cleared medical technology company focused on breast cancer prevention, built an agent that acted as domain expert across the engagement, supporting strategic pilot program design at multi-tiered facilities, distribution opportunity identification, and early flagging of insurance carrier friction.
data.OutcomeText: Better problem identification, opportunities surfaced that would not have come up otherwise, and concrete evidence in front of stakeholders early enough for alignment to be cheap.
data.RegisterNote: Emphasis is on how agents are used, not on the fact that he builds them. Do not lead with the tooling. The claim is that the strategy work is better, not that there are more agents.

data.Title: Startup work, concept to capital
data.ProblemText: Two early companies with real technology and no product story an outsider could buy.
data.ActionText: For an FDA cleared medical technology company focused on breast cancer prevention, led a pivot from a multi state Series A to a focused single state validation program and built the seed investor materials, shifting the narrative from detection to prevention. For an AI driven materials discovery company, translated lab technology into a customer facing platform through facilitation and interactive prototyping.
data.OutcomeText: Investor ready materials and a defined MVP path in both cases. Phase one delivered on the medical device engagement, with the strategy and investment direction in place.
data.AttributionNote: Neither client is named. Describe both by category. The medical technology engagement concluded after phase one due to internal changes on the client side.
data.RegisterNote: Covered on the resume via the m+d2 & Associates and Vortent Partners job entries rather than as a standalone Work page item.

data.Label: Variant A — Consulting and Advisory
data.AudienceDescription: Public. Linked from davidshadle.com, offered as a PDF download. Target length: two pages.
data.SummaryText:
I build the systems that turn strategy into working software. Most advisors stop at the recommendation. I keep going, through the model, the interface, and the handoff, so the thing that gets agreed on is the thing that gets shipped.

I start with the problem and write it down before anyone proposes a solution. From there I work from a rulebook: the rules of a domain written down once in plain language, with the technical pieces derived from that rather than maintained by hand. It is what lets me deliver complete projects rather than stopping at design and project management.

Twenty five years in product strategy and design make the systems worth building. Full stack product practitioner. Not just capable of wearing several hats at once, but confident delivering the outcome in each.

data.Label: Variant B — Principal and Director Roles
data.AudienceDescription: Sent directly for specific roles. Never published online. Conventional reverse-chronological structure for applicant tracking systems and hiring managers.
data.SummaryText:
Product strategy and design leader with twenty five years across enterprise platforms, cloud infrastructure, and early stage companies, including principal roles at Microsoft and Oracle. I define what to build and why, align the people who have to agree, and stay with the work through delivery.

I also build. Over the last two years I have designed and shipped a production platform end to end and implemented the experience layer across three executive reporting products. Working from a written rulebook rather than hand-maintained specs is what extended me from design and project management into complete delivery. That range means no handoff gap between strategy, design, and engineering.

Looking for defined ownership at a small to mid sized organization.
